name: Usable Security & Privacy
description: Human factors: user studies, mental models, warnings, and the usability of security and privacy tools.

ccs.narrative:
Research on usable security at CCS began taking shape around 2018, with early work concentrating on user-facing security, security UX, and human factors. (Un)informed Consent: Studying GDPR Consent Notices in the Field (CCS 2019) set an influential baseline by showing how to Field study of GDPR cookie consent notices on popular websites, showing dark patterns and consent fatigue. Parallel contributions—Matched and Mismatched SOCs: A Qualitative Study on Security Operations Center Issues (2019) and Investigating System Operators' Perspective on Security Misconfigurations (2018) —reinforced the foundational challenges in this space.

A productive wave of CCS work from 2020–2022 deepened the area. A Qualitative Study of Dependency Management and Its Security Implications (CCS 2020) advanced the field by demonstrating Qualitatively studies why developers fail to update vulnerable dependencies and the resulting software supply-chain.... Other strong contributions included "I need a better description": An Investigation Into User Expectations For Differential Privacy (2021), An Inside Look into the Practice of Malware Analysis (2021), broadening the space of techniques and targets.

The most recent CCS contributions (from 2023 onward) reflect a maturing field that pushes into harder targets and broader threat models. Do Users Write More Insecure Code with AI Assistants? (CCS 2023) exemplified this trend by tackling User study showing developers with AI code assistants tend to write more insecure code while believing it is secure. Similarly, Using AI Assistants in Software Development: A Qualitative Study on Security Practices and Concerns (2024) and "Get in Researchers; We're Measuring Reproducibility": A Reproducibility Study of Machine Learning Papers in Tier 1 Security Conferences (2023) show how the community continues to scale and adapt its methods.

uss.narrative:
Usable security and privacy research in this period began by zeroing in on the everyday tools and policies that mediate user decisions. The earliest listed work attacked the comprehension problem head-on: "Polisis: Automated Analysis and Presentation of Privacy Policies Using Deep Learning" (USENIX 2018) used machine learning to make impenetrable privacy policies queryable, while several password studies that same year -- "Better managed than memorized? Studying the Impact of Managers on Password Strength and Reuse" and "Forgetting of Passwords: Ecological Theory and Data" -- probed why authentication keeps failing users. At the same time, the field began stretching past the single user: "Rethinking Access Control and Authentication for the Home Internet of Things (IoT)" (USENIX 2018) argued that multi-user devices break the assumptions baked into traditional access control.

The major shift across 2019-2020 was a turn toward vulnerable and at-risk populations and the social context of security. "Clinical Computer Security for Victims of Intimate Partner Violence" (USENIX 2019) reframed security as something delivered through human-centered, clinical interventions, and was reinforced by work on human trafficking survivors and, in 2020, "The Tools and Tactics Used in Intimate Partner Surveillance" -- collectively establishing interpersonal abuse as a core research agenda. In parallel, the multi-user theme matured with "Understanding and Improving Security and Privacy in Multi-User Smart Homes" (USENIX 2019) and branched into emerging platforms via "Secure Multi-User Content Sharing for Augmented Reality Applications" (USENIX 2019). A second strand recognized that developers are users too: "Stack Overflow Considered Helpful! Deep Learning Security Nudges Towards Stronger Cryptography" (2019) and "Understanding security mistakes developers make" (2020) treated developer behavior as a usability problem in its own right.

By 2020-2021 the work scaled up and got more empirical, measuring real systems and large populations: "A Comprehensive Quality Evaluation of Security and Privacy Advice on the Web" (2020) audited the advice ecosystem, while "Empirical Measurement of Systemic 2FA Usability" (2020) and "Driving 2FA Adoption at Scale" (2021) moved authentication research from lab studies to deployment-scale optimization. Global and collective perspectives also emerged, from "A Large Scale Study of User Behavior, Expectations and Engagement with Android Permissions" (2021) to "Collective Information Security in Large-Scale Urban Protests: the Case of Hong Kong" (2021).

Most recently the area has confronted harder conceptual and methodological questions and new threat surfaces. "What Are the Chances? Explaining the Epsilon Parameter in Differential Privacy" (USENIX 2023) tackled the usability of an abstract mathematical privacy notion, and "Ethical Frameworks and Computer Security Trolley Problems" (2023) pushed the community to formalize how it reasons about research ethics. The at-risk and emerging-platform threads converged in "Abuse Vectors: A Framework for Conceptualizing IoT-Enabled Interpersonal Abuse" (2023) and "Exploring User Reactions and Mental Models Towards Perceptual Manipulation Attacks in Mixed Reality" (2023), showing the field now studies mental models against AI- and immersive-tech-driven threats like those in "DeepPhish" (2022). The trajectory runs from making existing tools and policies understandable, to centering vulnerable users and developers, to rigorous large-scale measurement, and finally to grappling with the usability and ethics of frontier privacy techniques and immersive systems.

top4.narrative:
The earliest papers in this list (all 2018) staked out the core terrain of usable security and privacy: making opaque systems legible to ordinary people and extending protection to populations that mainstream security ignores. On the legibility side, "Polisis: Automated Analysis and Presentation of Privacy Policies Using Deep Learning" (USENIX 2018) tried to turn unreadable privacy policies into something users could actually query, while "On the Accuracy of Password Strength Meters" (CCS 2018) scrutinized the everyday tools meant to nudge users toward better choices. At the same time the field began centering vulnerable and non-traditional users, with "The Spyware Used in Intimate Partner Violence" (S&P 2018) and "Computer Security and Privacy for Refugees in the United States" (S&P 2018) showing that threat models look very different for at-risk people. A parallel thread acknowledged that "users" are not just consumers but operators and developers, as in "Investigating System Operators' Perspective on Security Misconfigurations" (CCS 2018) and "Hackers vs. Testers: A Comparison of Software Vulnerability Discovery Processes" (S&P 2018).

Around 2019 the field matured methodologically and turned a hard eye on regulation and mental models. "How Well Do My Results Generalize? Comparing Security and Privacy Survey Results from MTurk, Web, and Telephone Samples" (S&P 2019) pushed researchers to question whether their convenient MTurk samples actually generalized, sharpening the rigor of the whole subfield. The GDPR's arrival produced "(Un)informed Consent: Studying GDPR Consent Notices in the Field" (CCS 2019), which empirically showed how consent banners manipulate rather than inform. Studies of mental models, like "If HTTPS Were Secure, I Wouldn't Need 2FA - End User and Administrator Mental Models of HTTPS" (S&P 2019), revealed how badly users' and admins' understanding diverges from reality. The intimate-partner-violence line deepened from observation into intervention with "Clinical Computer Security for Victims of Intimate Partner Violence" (USENIX 2019).

By 2020-2021 the work fanned out across new technologies and authentication paradigms while consolidating its understanding of harm. Authentication research moved beyond passwords toward hardware and passwordless schemes in "A Tale of Two Studies: The Best and Worst of YubiKey Usability" (S&P 2018) and "Is FIDO2 the Kingslayer of User Authentication?" (S&P 2020), and into VR with "OcuLock" (NDSS 2020). Emerging domains got their own usability treatments: IoT labeling in "Ask the Experts: What Should Be on an IoT Privacy and Security Label?" (S&P 2020), voice assistants in "Hey Alexa, is this Skill Safe?" (NDSS 2021), and a new focus on communicating abstract guarantees in "Towards Effective Differential Privacy Communication" (S&P 2020) and "I need a better description: An Investigation Into User Expectations For Differential Privacy" (CCS 2021). Developers as a security-critical user group came into sharper focus through "A Qualitative Study of Dependency Management and Its Security Implications" (CCS 2020) and "Understanding security mistakes developers make" (USENIX 2020).

Most recently the field has worked to unify its sprawling subfields and confront AI. "SoK: A Framework for Unifying At-Risk User Research" (S&P 2022) and "SoK: Hate, Harassment, and the Changing Landscape of Online Abuse" (S&P 2021) gathered a decade of fragmented studies of vulnerable users into shared frameworks, and "SoK: Authentication in Augmented and Virtual Reality" (S&P 2022) did the same for emerging-platform authentication. Large-scale field experiments like "Phishing in Organizations: Findings from a Large-Scale and Long-Term Study" (S&P 2022) brought ecological validity that earlier lab studies lacked. The newest frontier is the human-AI relationship in security, opened by "Do Users Write More Insecure Code with AI Assistants?" (CCS 2023), which asks whether the latest productivity tools quietly erode the security of what developers build. The arc, in short, runs from making existing systems understandable, to protecting marginalized users, to rigorous large-scale methods, and now to the security usability of AI itself.
